entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pekah, son of Remaliah, reigned as the eighteenth king of the Northern Kingdom of Israel from approximately 740 to 732 BCE, a tumultuous period marked by the ascendant power of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. His eight-year rule, described in 2 Kings 15:27-31 and Isaiah 7-9, was defined by a radical shift in foreign policy, abandoning a pro-Assyrian stance in favor of a desperate anti-Assyrian alliance. This decision, aimed at preserving Israel's sovereignty, ultimately provoked a devastating Assyrian response that irrevocably altered the geopolitical landscape of the Levant and set Israel on a path toward its final destruction.

Having served as a captain under his predecessor, King Pekahiah, Pekah seized the throne through a violent coup, assassinating Pekahiah in Samaria with the aid of fifty Gileadites. Immediately upon consolidating power, he forged a military alliance with King Rezin of Aram-Damascus, forming the core of the anti-Assyrian coalition. Together, they launched the Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 734-732 BCE), invading the Kingdom of Judah with the intent of dethroning King Ahaz and replacing him with a more compliant ruler, likely the 'son of Tabeel' mentioned in Isaiah 7:6. This aggressive maneuver was designed to force Judah into their anti-Assyrian front, thereby strengthening their collective resistance against Tiglath-Pileser III.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pekah's reign and his anti-Assyrian alliance directly triggered the devastating intervention of Tiglath-Pileser III, leading to the loss of most Israelite territory and mass deportations, thereby setting the stage for the final destruction of the Northern Kingdom a decade later.
